item.title: North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, US agencies say
item.description: Crypto firms have frozen about $2.7 billion of the stolen funds. Binance says user funds are safe and it will cover all losses.

item.title: New York Times sues Brave over paywall bypass and AI content sales
item.description: The paper says Brave sold its journalism through its Search API and shipped a default paywall blocker. Other newspapers have filed their own suits in the same court.

item.title: Reporters Without Borders names Trump a press freedom predator
item.description: The group put him in its 2026 gallery of 33. The United States fell seven places to 64th of 180 countries.

item.title: French minister Darmanin warns Le Pen or Mélenchon win would end the EU
item.description: He told an audience in Barcelona a win for either would leave no European Community. The RN wants to cut France's 30.9 billion euro EU contribution the most, Le Figaro reports. France votes for president on 18 April.

item.title: EU split over strict checks on foreign IT suppliers ahead of Parliament debate
item.description: Member states want to keep the decisions for themselves. MEPs debate cyber resilience and critical infrastructure on Wednesday at 15:00.

item.title: Commission proposes €4.2 billion for Hungary and full Erasmus access
item.description: The Council has one month to decide on lifting the 2022 measures, which would also restore Hungarian access to Horizon Europe.

item.title: Poland caught up fast in the EU. The bill now sits on Warsaw's books.
item.description: Two decades of membership closed much of the gap with the EU, but the euros did less of that work than the price tag suggests. The deficits and debt are Poland's own, and the next round of costs is still up for grabs.

item.title: Hackers hit supermarket fridges across Europe again
item.description: The second attack in three weeks hit stores in France, Belgium, Sweden and the Netherlands. Intermarché's chief says France alone faces losses of tens of millions of euros in a day.

item.title: US troops and NATO cash on the line as Trump warns allies
item.description: The Pentagon has cancelled a brigade rotation to Poland and plans fewer troops in Germany, and diplomats fear more after the midterms. The White House points to the 5 percent spending deal.

item.title: Belgian government nears collapse over 10 billion euro budget hole
item.description: King Philippe is considering Prime Minister De Wever's resignation. If he accepts it, elections must follow within forty days.

item.title: EU and Canada agree deal short of membership
item.description: Diplomats say the deal drops the 'associate member' label Canada wanted, after Germany objected. It promises fewer trade barriers and a study on more Canadian LNG exports to Europe.

item.title: Hackers send false missile alerts through Ukraine's air warning app
item.description: The Air Alert app reached about 6.7 million users before developers shut it down and restored it within two hours. A Russian emergency ministry app was hit the next night.

item.title: Court orders Russian hockey teams back. Finland and Latvia refuse to play
item.description: The ruling covers all tournaments, including the 2027 World Championship in Germany. Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen says she will move to block Russian athletes from entering Finland.

item.title: Russia lost ground in October and took its heaviest losses of the war
item.description: Ukraine counted 54,400 Russian soldiers killed or wounded in one month. Russian forces advanced only in the Sumy and Zaporizhia regions.

item.title: Coalition to test moving troops into Ukraine in Polish drills
item.description: The Koalicja exercise at Nowa Dęba starts on 9 November. Le Monde reports almost 3,000 soldiers; RMF24 says nearly 5,000. At its end, the Ukraine force command moves from Paris to London.

item.title: Russia leaves European anti-torture convention, ending prison oversight
item.description: The Council of Europe's monitoring committee can no longer enter Russian prisons or detention places. It visited over 450 sites there between 1998 and 2021.

item.title: Dutch MP wants ban on addictive app design, with off-switch for repeat offenders
item.description: The PvdA bill would fine platforms for tricks like endless scrolling, then pull the plug. Kathmann coordinates rules with MPs in seven other countries.

item.title: Brussels pauses national social media bans for children for a year
item.description: The freeze covers Austria's planned ban and runs to 28 July 2027. The Commission wants member states to back its EU-wide Kids Act instead.

item.title: Nuclear strike claim on Iran rests on one unnamed source
item.description: Tucker Carlson says an attack may be days away. Trump said on October 16 he would not use nuclear weapons, and the White House keeps all options open.

item.title: Half a million march in France over cost of living, police arrest 565
item.description: Clashes marked the third day of protests in Paris, Marseille and Lyon. Police put 70,000 officers on the streets.

item.title: Belgian government resigns amid 10 billion euro budget gap
item.description: MR walked out over a capital gains tax and a financial transaction tax. Belgium's deficit hit 5.2% of GDP in 2025.

item.title: Poland's constitutional crisis deepens as police ring the Tribunal
item.description: President Nawrocki cut short a trip to Senegal and called the seizure of the court a break with constitutional order. Prime Minister Tusk said in a national address that no politician, not even the president, may enter a court or pressure judges.

item.title: EU funds lifted Poland, but most of the growth came from elsewhere
item.description: Two decades of membership brought 181 billion euro net and growth far above the EU average. The funds' own figures credit only a small share of it, and the bill for the next budget round is being set now.

item.title: Ukraine's refinery strikes cost Russia at home while export cargoes kept moving
item.description: The strikes cut half of Russia's refining capacity and pushed fuel prices up inside the country. Crude exports held the line, so the cost has not landed on the ships leaving Russian ports.

item.title: Le Pen leads France's first-round poll at 33.5 percent, Attal calls for primary
item.description: Ipsos puts Attal at 17 percent and Mélenchon at 15. Retailleau rejected the primary, saying it would only help Le Pen.

item.title: Man charged with spying in Poland held for three months over rail photos
item.description: Police found several hundred thousand files, mainly of railway, airport and telecoms sites in Poland and abroad, plus four Russian passports. The case now goes to prosecutors in Wrocław.

item.title: Mayor warns riot-hit shops of lost economic existence
item.description: One shop owner near the Konstablerwache puts his damage at 30,000 to 40,000 euros and reopens Monday. More than 100 officers were hurt after Halloween-night looting on the Zeil.

item.title: EU opens consultation on AI Act enforcement rules
item.description: Companies can send views to the European Commission until 9 November. Fines reach 35 million euros for banned AI practices.

item.title: Reform UK builds seven-day Westminster newsroom with studio and news desk
item.description: The party is hiring at least 12 staff and has built a Westminster video studio for the launch of Reform TV on YouTube, with a paper it says will reach 15 million homes.

item.title: Cost of living protests hit France and Germany; Frankfurt shops looted
item.description: French police arrested 565 people in a third round of demonstrations. German police used water cannon at the marches. Shops in Cologne and Düsseldorf barricaded; Frankfurt shops looted.
